assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED showed that a superconducting artificial atom can be strongly and controllably coupled to a single microwave photon in a resonator, opening a new regime of light-matter physics on a chip. It gave dispersive readout, the transmon-resonator architecture, and the platform for much of today's quantum-information experiments. It is a clean case of foundational quantum optics turning into an enabling platform, and every superconducting-qubit group reproduces it.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 theory proposal (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf) and the first strong-coupling experiment (Wallraff et al., Schoelkopf group) are the decisive steps. Blais, Girvin and Schoelkopf cover theory and experiment. Credit is shared with Wallraff and with the Yale co-authors who are not on this list, so the triple omits some real contributors. Devoret and Martinis were honored in 2025 for the tunnelling and circuit work, which makes this an adjacent but distinct discovery.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently confirmed in many laboratories over about 20 years. Reproducibility and robustness are not in doubt. Recognition is timely, following the 2025 prize and fitting within the same field.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2025 prize could be read as too close to it; I weigh this as separate physics, but colleagues may disagree.
Allocation among Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and Wallraff is debatable; Wallraff is not in the credited names.
As director of a superconducting-circuits programme I have a possible conflict of interest and would defer to colleagues on this candidate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock combines the magic-wavelength idea with many atoms interrogated at once. It brought fractional uncertainty to the 10^-18 level and is a real step in precision, enabling tests of relativity, searches for fundamental-constant drift and relativistic geodesy. The idea is original, clear and clean to describe.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice clock and realized the first one. Ye's group made the decisive demonstrations of ultra-high coherence and accuracy with Sr. Together these two make a natural pair. Others, such as Hall and Hänsch for combs (2005) and Lemonde, are connected but are not on the list.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many groups (JILA, RIKEN, PTB, NIST, SYRTE, and others). The redefinition of the second is under discussion, which makes timing favorable and not premature.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to treat this as an extension of the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
Credit for the early lattice-clock proposals beyond Katori is not fully clear to me.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realize Hubbard-type models with tunable parameters, including the superfluid to Mott insulator transition, and quantum gas microscopes with single-site resolution. They gave a new way to study strongly correlated matter and opened the field of analog quantum simulation. The ability to see and control a basic quantum phenomenon in detail is exactly what I value.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch) supplied the key theory proposal. Greiner and Bloch showed the Mott transition (2002) and later developed single-site imaging. Esslinger's fermionic Hubbard work and Hänsch's role are also relevant. Four names are credited, and the best triple is not clear, because Jaksch and Hänsch contributed but are not eligible here.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature and reproduced widely. The experiments have an established record. The extent to which quantum simulators answer open physics questions is still developing, but the underlying discovery is stable.
uncertainties: The choice of three out of Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger and Zoller is hard and could be disputed.
Overlap with B014 and B039 means only one of these may be appropriate for the same year.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics reached the quantum regime of mechanical motion, with ground-state cooling, radiation-pressure effects at the quantum level, and optomechanical entanglement. It links to my own area through microwave optomechanics and shows quantum physics in macroscopic objects, with strong links to the 2025 theme. LIGO-type sensing benefits as well.
assessment.attribution: Aspelmeyer, Kippenberg and Vahala made the key early demonstrations of radiation-pressure back-action and cooling in optical microcavities. Quantum ground-state cooling was done in several groups, including Painter, Teufel, Lehnert and Cleland, who are not in the credited set. This weakens the attribution for a clean prize.
assessment.maturity: Experimental results are robust across platforms. The field is still moving, so the clearest discovery within it is not yet singled out, and the case may be somewhat premature.
uncertainties: Credit is spread over many groups and platforms (optical, microwave, mechanical).
It is unclear what single discovery would be named in the prize citation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of flat bands at the magic angle and their experimental observation, giving correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene, opened moiré quantum matter. It is original, high-impact and has produced a large new field. A clear new regime of physics was opened.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the 2011 theory; Cao, Jarillo-Herrero and colleagues made the 2018 experiments. The attribution is relatively clean, though Cao as first author and others (Dean, Young) also contributed.
assessment.maturity: Strongly reproduced, but the understanding of the superconducting mechanism is not settled. Recognition is somewhat early, though consensus on the flat-band discovery is solid.
uncertainties: The nature of superconductivity in magic-angle graphene is still debated.
Possibly premature while the mechanism is unresolved.
Outside my main expertise; I defer to condensed-matter colleagues.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cirac and Zoller proposed the trapped-ion quantum gate and laid out the theory for quantum computing and simulation with ions and neutral atoms. The ideas are foundational, original and have been realized experimentally in many laboratories.
assessment.attribution: The proposal (1995) is clearly theirs. The pair is natural and compact. Experimental realization by Wineland's group and Blatt and others means the experimental side is partly covered by the 2012 prize (Wineland).
assessment.maturity: Mature and confirmed by decades of trapped-ion and neutral-atom experiments. Timing is acceptable, but part of the field has already been recognized.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize (Wineland, Haroche) for ion control, and with candidates B010 and B023.
The theory-only recognition may be considered less appropriate than recognition of the experiments.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade and programmable neutral-atom arrays enable fast entangling gates and large-scale quantum simulation with single-atom control. The experiments reached a new regime with hundreds of atoms and entangling operations of high fidelity.
assessment.attribution: The Rydberg blockade proposal (Jaksch, Lukin, Zoller and coworkers) and the first demonstrations (Browaeys, Saffman and others) are the decisive steps; the array and tweezers work involves Lukin, Greiner, Browaeys and Bernien, as well as Zoller's theory. The three credited names cover only part of this.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly developing, with strong confirmation by several groups, but a stable interpretation and the full impact are still being worked out. It may well be premature compared with older candidates.
uncertainties: Probably premature, since fidelities and error correction in these systems are still advancing.
Several decisive contributors (Zoller, Jaksch, Greiner, Ahn) are outside the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light reduces quantum noise below the standard quantum limit, and it now improves gravitational-wave detectors. The theoretical proposal and first observation are conceptually clear and have a lasting impact, and I know squeezing from microwave circuits as well.
assessment.attribution: Caves provided the theory of squeezed-light interferometry; Kimble's group observed squeezing in 1986 (Slusher at Bell Labs was first, and Wu, Kimble and others also contributed). Schnabel's role is in applying it to the GEO600 detector. Slusher and Walls are not in the credited list, so the credit is incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed and used in operating detectors (GEO600, LIGO, Virgo). It is mature, and timing is helped by the gravitational-wave applications, although LIGO already was recognized in 2017.
uncertainties: Priority of the first observation (Slusher et al. 1985) leaves attribution unresolved.
The discovery may be seen as an enabling technique more than a discovery of new physics.
